content:
India and the United States have all but finished negotiating their long-awaited trade agreement, but the deal will not be signed until Washington rebuilds the tariff system on which it was supposed to rest, India's top trade official said on Wednesday.

Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told an event organised by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) in New Delhi that the legal text of the first tranche of the bilateral trade agreement is in its final stages and that negotiations will conclude soon. The signing, however, is a different matter. According to [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/business/Economy/india-us-trade-deal-signing-will-still-take-some-time-says-commerce-secretary-rajesh-agrawal/article71715672.ece), Agrawal said the agreement would still take some time to sign, because it can only be concluded once the United States has settled its new tariff architecture.

The problem is one of timing, not of substance. When India and the United States announced the framework of an interim trade deal in February, it was negotiated against the backdrop of the executive tariff system put in place by President Donald Trump, under which Indian goods faced a tariff of 50 per cent. Later that month, the US Supreme Court struck down the legal foundation of those tariffs, which had been imposed under emergency powers. Washington is now building a replacement tariff structure from scratch, and until that structure is in place, neither side can fix the terms of a deal in law.

Now a new tariff architecture is being created by the US, Agrawal said at the FICCI event. Until that tariff architecture comes back in place, the signing of a deal is something that I think will take some time.

The February framework itself was generous by the standards of the tariff war that preceded it. Announced on 7 February, it committed Washington to applying an 18 per cent reciprocal tariff on Indian goods covered by the arrangement, down from 25 per cent, and to rolling back a further 25 per cent penalty tariff that had been imposed over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil. That headline, widely reported at the time, is now in limbo: the rates were set against a tariff regime that no longer exists, and the replacement regime may price Indian goods differently.

A second obstacle is running in parallel. The US administration has opened investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the statute that allows Washington to impose duties in response to foreign trade practices it deems unfair. One of those investigations, into forced labour, has already been completed, and a tariff of 10 per cent has been levied on imports from India. A second investigation, into excess industrial capacity, is still under way and could bring further tariffs. According to NDTV Profit, the findings are expected over the coming weeks and months, which makes it difficult for either side to finalise an agreement while the potential tariff implications remain unclear.

The uncertainty matters because a trade deal is, above all, a promise of predictability. As The Hindu BusinessLine reported, comparative advantages offered to different countries need to be clear before a deal is signed, and every country would want an agreement that provides certainty on the Section 301 probes. Until Washington knows what duties the investigations will produce, it cannot tell New Delhi — or any other partner — what tariff rate its goods will ultimately face. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said the US has acknowledged that India will receive lower tariffs than its competitors, but that assurance has yet to be written into a signed text.

For Indian exporters, the delay means months more of operating without a firm answer on the cost of selling into the American market, their largest single destination. Businesses that had begun planning around the February framework — the 18 per cent rate and the removal of the Russian-oil penalty — must now wait for a new tariff architecture whose shape is still being drawn up in Washington.

The stakes extend beyond the bilateral relationship. The same tariff uncertainty is reshaping trade diplomacy across Asia: leaders gathering in Shenzhen this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit have been pressing for open markets and clearer rules, and China and Canada used the occasion to agree deeper tariff relief of their own, as reported in [China and Canada agree deeper tariff cuts as Xi and Carney meet in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-carney-tariff-cuts-shenzhen-november-2026). Regional leaders also met in Manila this week to coordinate on trade and security, a sign of how quickly governments are moving to hedge against Washington's shifting tariff landscape, as covered in [Quad leaders meet in Manila for first time in more than two years](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/quad-leaders-manila-summit-november-2026).

Agrawal struck an upbeat note on the substance of the talks. Every aspect of the deal has been more or less finalised, and we will be concluding the negotiations soon, he said, according to Outlook India. The legal agreement, he added, has also been negotiated and is now in its final stages. The message from New Delhi is that the hard bargaining is done; what remains is for Washington to decide, through its courts, its investigations and its new tariff architecture, what the deal it has already negotiated is actually worth.

No date has been set for the signing, and none is likely until the Section 301 findings land and the new US tariff framework takes shape. For now, the agreement exists in draft, the tariffs exist in flux, and the world's two largest democracies are waiting on the same thing: a tariff system that stays still long enough to sign.
summary: India says its trade deal with the United States is virtually negotiated, but the signing must wait until Washington rebuilds the tariff system the US Supreme Court struck down in February, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Wednesday.
title: India-US trade deal signing delayed as Washington rebuilds its tariff system
